caption_hook: Wyoming has a supervolcano, a tower of cooled magma, ancient fish lakes and some of the oldest rock around.

layers.name: LAVA CREEK TUFF
layers.what: Yellowstone's most recent giant eruption spread hot ash across much of North America. It left a vast crater, called a caldera, roughly 30 by 45 miles across.
layers.bonus: The heat still left under it powers Yellowstone's geysers and hot springs.

layers.name: DEVILS TOWER
layers.what: Molten rock pushed into older layers and cooled slowly, cracking into six-sided columns. Erosion stripped away the softer rock and left the tower rising 867 ft from its base.
layers.bonus: In 1906 it became the first national monument in the United States.

layers.name: GREEN RIVER FORMATION
layers.what: Warm, calm lakes once covered southwest Wyoming. Their fine mud preserved fish, turtles, crocodiles, bats and palm leaves in astonishing detail, now split from slabs of stone.
layers.bonus: Nearby, Wyoming sits on the world's largest known deposit of trona, used to make glass.

layers.name: MORRISON FORMATION
layers.what: Rivers, swamps and mudflats where the biggest dinosaurs ever lived left bones by the ton. Wyoming's quarries here have supplied museums around the world.
layers.bonus: A shepherd near Como Bluff once built a cabin out of dinosaur bones.

layers.name: TENSLEEP SANDSTONE
layers.what: Sandy beaches and wind-blown dunes at the edge of a shallow sea turned to tough stone. It is named for the town of Ten Sleep in the Bighorn Mountains.
layers.bonus: Its porous sand is also a major oil reservoir under Wyoming's basins.

layers.name: THE BASEMENT
layers.hook: The ancient core of a continent
layers.what: Beneath Wyoming lies some of the oldest crust in North America. In the Tetons, banded gneiss about 2.7 billion years old was lifted into the sharp peaks of Grand Teton.
layers.bonus: The rock is ancient, but the Teton peaks began rising less than 10 million years ago.
